title: DECISION MAKING AND PROBLEM SOLVING IN EXTENSION ORGANISATIONS
text:
Welcome
Welcome to Decision Making and Problem Solving in Extension Organisations, the online course book for the Post Graduate Diploma in Agricultural Extension Management (PGDAEM) offered through the Central Training Institute, Mannuthy, Kerala Agricultural University.
Every extension worker is, at heart, a decision maker and a problem solver. Which programme should be funded this year? Why did farmers not adopt a technology that worked so well in on-station trials? How should a team respond to a pest outbreak that no recommendation yet covers? This book brings together the concepts, theories, models and tools that help extension managers answer such questions systematically rather than by habit or guesswork.

About this book
The book is organised in three parts. Part I introduces decision making in agriculture and extension organisations, its cognitive basis, decision making under certainty, risk and uncertainty, group decision making and the main theories of decision making. Part II covers the methodologies used to structure decisions. Part III deals with problem solving: its nature in agriculture and extension, process frameworks, classic models, organisational and creativity-based techniques, and the statistical and graphical tools used to diagnose problems.


How to use this book

Read each chapter before the corresponding class (see the class schedule in About the course), so that class time can be spent on discussion and exercises.
Work through the agricultural examples and case studies in the shaded boxes; they show how each idea applies in the field.
Use the Chapter Summary at the end of each chapter for revision. Answers to the fill-in-the-blank questions are given at the end of every chapter.

title: About the course

How the book is organised
Part I (Decision Making) begins with what a decision is and how decisions are classified on farms and in extension organisations (1  Decision making in agriculture and extension organisations). It then turns to the mental processes behind decisions and to the rules that apply when outcomes are certain, risky or uncertain (2  Cognition and decision making under certainty, risk and uncertainty), and closes with group decision making and the major theories that explain how farmers and organisations actually decide (3  Group decision making and theories of decision making).
Part II (Methodologies for Decision Making) describes the practical methods used to structure decisions: decision trees, the Delphi technique, brainstorming, the fishbone diagram, data-driven decision making and decision support systems (4  Methodologies for decision making in extension organisations).
Part III (Problem Solving) defines a problem and examines the problems extension workers face (5  Problem solving in agriculture and extension organisations), presents classic models and organisational and creative techniques for solving them (6  Theories, models and techniques for problem solving), and ends with the statistical and graphical tools of quality improvement and the E5 framework for organisational problem solving (7  Statistical and graphical methods and the E5 framework for problem solving).
Several tools, notably brainstorming and the fishbone diagram, appear in both the decision-making and the problem-solving parts. The cross-references in the text point to the section where each is treated in full.

title: 1  Decision making in agriculture and extension organisations
text:
1.1 What is decision making?
This chapter introduces decision making as a process, examines how decisions are made on farms and in agricultural extension organisations, and classifies agricultural decisions by time horizon, complexity and uncertainty.
Decision making is the cognitive, rational process of selecting the best course of action from multiple alternatives to achieve a specific goal. It involves identifying problems, evaluating options and committing to a path of action (Van den Ban & Hawkins, 1996). In agriculture, this process is shaped not only by economics but also by personal experience, social influences and access to information.

1.2 The seven-step decision-making process
Decision making can be described as a sequence of seven steps (Figure 1.1):

Define the problem: clearly identify the issue requiring resolution or the goal to be achieved.
Gather relevant information: collect internal and external data, including market research, expert opinions and past experiences.
Identify alternatives: develop a range of possible, actionable solutions or options.
Weigh the evidence: evaluate the pros and cons of each alternative, assessing potential risks and benefits.
Choose the best option: select the most suitable alternative that best fulfils the objective.
Take action: put the chosen plan into action by allocating resources and assigning tasks.
Review the decision: evaluate the outcome, analyse consequences and determine whether the problem was resolved.

1.3 Decision making in agriculture
Agricultural decision making is a complex process influenced by economic, environmental and social factors. It is a behavioural process in which farmers and agribusiness stakeholders evaluate available information, consider alternatives and choose actions that best align with their goals (Van den Ban & Hawkins, 1996). Decision making in farm households is not solely the responsibility of the male head — other family members may be involved, and some decisions are made collectively.
One critical decision is whether to adopt new technologies: improved seeds, fertilisers, agrochemicals and mechanisation. Determining profitability requires farm-specific information (such as soil tests) as well as insights from neighbouring farmers who have already adopted.

1.4 Decision making in agricultural extension organisations
Decision making in extension organisations is inherently complex because of diverse farmer needs, variable environmental conditions, evolving market dynamics and policy constraints (Leeuwis & Van den Ban, 2004). An Agricultural Decision Making Support System (ADSS) integrates agricultural information systems, simulation models and expert systems to enable extension agents to deliver precise, real-time and customised guidance. Decision support systems are discussed further in Section 4.6.

1.5.2 Classification by complexity

Routine (low complexity): repetitive, everyday decisions made from habit, past experience or standard practice. They require little new information or analysis.
Tactical (moderate complexity): decisions that require some planning and assessment, affect operations for a season or a few years, and involve evaluating different options.
Strategic (high complexity): long-term, high-impact decisions that require significant information gathering, expert consultation and analysis, and involve large financial investments with lasting consequences.

title: 2  Cognition and decision making under certainty, risk and uncertainty
text:
2.1 Cognitive structures and functions in agricultural decision making
This chapter examines the mental structures and functions that underlie farmers’ decisions, three approaches to operational decision making, and the theories and decision rules that apply when outcomes are certain, risky or uncertain.
Effective agricultural decision making involves internal cognitive structures — the mental representations that store farmers’ beliefs, goals, plans and preferences. These structures are actively manipulated by several higher-level cognitive functions (Jager et al., 2000).
crumbs: 2  Cognition and decision making under certainty, risk and uncertainty

title: 2  Cognition and decision making under certainty, risk and uncertainty
text:
2.1.1 Core cognitive functions

Attention and perception: farmers decide what to focus on within their production system, identifying which information is most relevant and how best to access it.
Sense-making and interpretation: by interpreting cues — changes in weather, crop health or market signals — farmers recognise abnormal patterns, form beliefs or predictions, and draw parallels with previous experiences (Weick, 1995).
Memory and recall: remembering critical facts, events and sequences helps farmers compare past outcomes with current scenarios, forming the basis for future decisions.
Goal formulation and selection: farmers set specific objectives based on their assessment of the situation, which then guides subsequent decision-making steps (Bratman, 1987).
Plan generation and adaptation: farmers generate or adjust plans that align with their goals, considering strategies that can be implemented under current circumstances.
Plan evaluation through mental simulation: before executing a plan, farmers mentally simulate its outcomes — essentially assessing the potential success of the strategy (Klein, 1998).
Action selection: a final action is chosen based on the plans developed, existing goals and current preferences.

text:
2.2 Three approaches to operational decision making

2.2.1 The Decision Ladder
The Decision Ladder (DL) visually maps how decision makers progress through stages when solving a problem (Rasmussen, 1976). Nodes represent specific steps in the process; links illustrate the logical flow between steps — from analysing the situation, through defining a target and planning a course of action, to executing it. Experts may skip certain steps using heuristics, allowing quicker, more efficient decisions.


2.2.2 Recognition-Primed Decision making
The Recognition-Primed Decision (RPD) model describes how experienced individuals make rapid yet effective decisions in real-world, high-pressure environments (Klein, 1998). Rather than evaluating multiple options through detailed comparisons, experienced decision makers recognise patterns from past experience and apply previously successful solutions. Its key aspects are:

Pattern recognition: a mental ‘library’ of situations;
Situational awareness: perceiving key details and predicting how the situation may evolve; and
Mental simulation: mentally testing actions to predict outcomes when an immediate solution is not clear.



2.2.3 The Belief–Desire–Intention (BDI) model
The BDI model posits that deliberation and means–ends reasoning operate through three components (Bratman, 1987):

Beliefs: the agent’s perception of the world, continuously updated through sensory input;
Desires: the agent’s goals — the driving force behind decision making; and
Intentions: specific commitments to actions selected from among desires, focusing cognitive resources on a feasible course of action.

The framework operates dynamically, iteratively generating and refining goals, formulating plans and guiding action selection.

title: 2  Cognition and decision making under certainty, risk and uncertainty
text:
2.3 Decision making under certainty
Decision making under certainty occurs when farmers or agricultural managers have complete knowledge of the outcomes of their decisions. Outcomes are predictable, information is reliable and risk is low (Hardaker et al., 2015). Examples include irrigation management based on well-established scheduling, and crop selection in controlled greenhouse environments where temperature, humidity and nutrients are managed to ensure predictable yields.

2.3.1 Theories of decision making under certainty

Rational choice theory: individuals make logical, informed decisions by selecting the option that maximises benefits and minimises costs (Arrow, 1951). Its assumptions are full information, maximisation of utility and consistency. Its limitation is that it does not account for psychological factors, emotions or biases, and it assumes perfect information, which is rare in practice. The theory is discussed further in Section 3.5.1.
Linear programming and decision trees: mathematical models used to determine the best course of action given resource constraints (Hardaker et al., 2015). Linear programming maximises profit or minimises cost; decision trees provide a graphical representation of decision paths with certain outcomes (see Section 4.1.2).

title: 2  Cognition and decision making under certainty, risk and uncertainty
text:
2.4 Decision making under risk
Under risk, outcomes are not certain but their probabilities can be estimated. The key framework is Expected Utility Theory (von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944), which holds that rational decision makers choose the option with the highest expected utility — the probability-weighted sum of utility values across all possible outcomes.
crumbs: 2  Cognition and decision making under certainty, risk and uncertainty

title: 2  Cognition and decision making under certainty, risk and uncertainty
text:
2.5 Decision making under uncertainty
Under uncertainty, outcomes cannot be estimated with known probabilities. Decision rules commonly applied include:

Maximin: maximise the minimum possible payoff (the most conservative rule);
Maximax: maximise the maximum possible payoff (the most optimistic rule); and
Minimax regret: minimise the maximum possible regret from a suboptimal choice.

In agriculture, uncertainty arises from erratic rainfall, new pest species, volatile markets and policy changes.
crumbs: 2  Cognition and decision making under certainty, risk and uncertainty

title: 2  Cognition and decision making under certainty, risk and uncertainty
text:
2.6 Prospect theory
Prospect Theory provides a behavioural alternative to Expected Utility Theory, demonstrating that people evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point (e.g., current income) rather than in absolute terms (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). Losses loom approximately twice as large as equivalent gains — a phenomenon known as loss aversion. This explains why farmers may resist adopting practices with higher expected yields if adoption carries any risk of performing worse than their current practice.

title: 3  Group decision making and theories of decision making
text:
3.1 Why group decision making matters in extension
This chapter examines why and how groups make decisions in extension organisations, the strategies available to extension managers, and the main theories that explain how farmers and organisations actually decide.
Many of the most consequential decisions in agricultural extension — programme prioritisation, community intervention design, technology assessment — involve multiple stakeholders with diverse interests, knowledge bases and risk tolerances. Group decision-making processes, when well structured, harness this diversity to produce more robust decisions and generate the shared ownership essential for implementation (Leeuwis & Van den Ban, 2004).

text:
3.4 Groupthink and its prevention
Groupthink occurs when the desire for harmony or conformity in a group overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives (Janis, 1982). Its symptoms include an illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalisation, pressure on dissenters and self-censorship. Prevention strategies include explicitly assigning a ‘devil’s advocate’ role, inviting external perspectives, allowing anonymous idea submission, and requiring each member to critically evaluate proposals before the final meeting.

title: 3  Group decision making and theories of decision making
text:
3.5 Theories of decision making

3.5.1 Rational Choice Theory
Rational Choice Theory (RCT) holds that an actor identifies alternative actions, determines their consequences and chooses the option that optimally satisfies their preferences — specifically, the option with the highest expected utility (Arrow, 1951). Its meta-theoretical foundation is methodological individualism: social facts result from the interaction and aggregation of individual rational actors (Boudon & Betton, 1999). In farming, the primary objective is typically taken to be income maximisation (Edwards-Jones, 2006).






Case study: Organic farming as rational choice



Best (2009) conducted a postal survey of 657 farmers in western Germany to test a rational choice model of organic farming adoption using Subjective Expected Utility (SEU) theory.
Result: Subjectively expected utility explained the adoption decision well. Non-tangible consequences (daily working conditions, identity) were as relevant as financial returns.
Implication: Extension advisers must present technologies in terms of the full range of subjective values that farmers hold, not only economic returns.




3.5.2 Bounded rationality
H. A. Simon (Nobel Prize, 1978) introduced bounded rationality as a departure from RCT. Decision makers are constrained by limited information, limited cognitive processing capacity and limited time. As a result, they tend to satisfice — choosing options that are ‘good enough’ relative to an aspiration threshold — rather than optimise (Simon, 1955). Studies consistently show that bounded rationality provides a more realistic description of actual farmer decision making than perfect rationality (Wens et al., 2020).

Satisficing
The satisficing heuristic combines ‘satisfy’ and ‘suffice’. Rather than pursuing the absolute best option, the decision maker searches sequentially through alternatives and stops when one meets the aspiration threshold. For example, a household evaluating livelihood options stops searching when the first option guarantees at least 1,830 calories per person per day — the minimum food security threshold.


Fast and frugal decision-tree heuristics
Bounded rationality is also expressed through fast and frugal decision trees — simplified, rule-based methods that evaluate specific criteria in a predetermined sequence (Gigerenzer & Selten, 2001). Decision makers consider only selected pieces of information, opting for efficient shortcuts rather than exhaustive analysis. These heuristics are ecologically rational — they perform well because they are adapted to the statistical structure of their natural decision environment.



3.5.3 Theory of Planned Behaviour
The Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) proposes that behaviour is determined by behavioural intentions, which are in turn shaped by three components (Ajzen, 1991) (Figure 3.1):

Attitude: a positive or negative evaluation of performing the behaviour;
Subjective norms: perceived social pressure from important others; and
Perceived behavioural control: perception of the ease or difficulty of performing the behaviour.

TPB has been widely applied in agricultural extension research to predict farmers’ adoption intentions for new technologies and conservation practices.


3.5.4 Diffusion of Innovations theory
Rogers (2003) conceptualises technology adoption as a decision-making process unfolding across five stages: knowledge, persuasion, decision, implementation and confirmation. Farmers are classified as innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority or laggards based on adoption timing. Extension agents must understand the characteristics and information needs of each adopter category to design appropriate communication and advisory strategies.

4.1 Decision analysis and decision trees
This chapter describes the main methodologies used to structure decisions in agriculture and extension organisations: decision analysis and decision trees, the Delphi technique, brainstorming, the cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram, data-driven decision making and decision support systems.

title: 4  Methodologies for decision making in extension organisations
text:
4.1.1 Decision analysis
Decision analysis is the systematic evaluation of alternatives using quantitative and qualitative tools. It involves defining objectives, identifying alternatives, assessing outcomes and selecting the best option (Hardaker et al., 2015). Decision analysis is applied both at farm level — deciding which crop to grow — and at organisational level — determining which extension programme to fund.


4.1.2 The decision tree
A decision tree is a visual, tree-shaped diagram that maps decisions, chance events and their possible outcomes. Its key components are:

Decision nodes (squares) — where the decision maker chooses among alternatives;
Chance nodes (circles) — where outcomes depend on probability;
Branches — representing decisions or chance outcomes; and
Terminal nodes — end points showing the final payoff.



4.1.3 Method

Define the decision problem clearly.
Identify all possible decision alternatives.
Identify chance events and assign probabilities.
Assign monetary values or utility scores to each terminal node.
Calculate the Expected Monetary Value (EMV): multiply each probability by its outcome value and sum the products.
Select the decision branch with the highest EMV.







Agricultural example: to irrigate or not



A farmer decides whether to irrigate paddy or rely on rainfall (Figure 4.1).

Irrigation: cost Rs. 5,000; guaranteed yield of 4 t/ha regardless of rain.
Rainfall: 60% chance of adequate rain (yield 3.5 t/ha; revenue Rs. 35,000) and 40% chance of drought (yield 1.5 t/ha; revenue Rs. 15,000).

EMV of relying on rainfall = (0.6 × 35,000) + (0.4 × 15,000) = Rs. 21,000 + Rs. 6,000 = Rs. 27,000.
At the same price (Rs. 10,000 per tonne), irrigation gives a certain revenue of Rs. 40,000, or Rs. 35,000 net of its cost. The decision tree allows the farmer to compare the two branches directly; in this example irrigation is the better choice.

4.2 The Delphi technique
The Delphi technique is a structured expert consultation method used to achieve consensus on complex issues through multiple rounds of anonymous questionnaires (Linstone & Turoff, 1975). It is particularly useful when there is no single correct answer and when expert judgement is required to address a question on which objective data are scarce.

4.2.1 Method

Define the problem or question clearly.
Select a panel of relevant experts (farmers, scientists, extension specialists, policymakers).
Distribute the Round 1 questionnaire anonymously.
Analyse responses and identify areas of agreement and disagreement.
Prepare a feedback summary and distribute the Round 2 questionnaire.
Repeat rounds until consensus emerges or positions stabilise.
Compile a final report reflecting consensus or documented divergence.

text:
4.3 Brainstorming in decision making
Brainstorming — covered in detail as a problem-solving technique in Section 6.4.2 — is also used as a decision-making technique when generating decision alternatives, identifying barriers to adoption and developing extension programme ideas. Its core rules are to defer judgement, encourage wild ideas, build on others’ ideas and go for quantity (Osborn, 1953). In extension it is used for identifying new programme approaches, solving field problems encountered by agents, staff planning and annual review sessions, and identifying barriers to technology adoption.

title: 4  Methodologies for decision making in extension organisations
text:
4.4 Cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram in decision making
The fishbone diagram — also covered as a problem-solving tool in Section 7.7 — serves a complementary role in decision making by structuring the diagnosis of why a decision problem exists (Ishikawa, 1990). Using the 6M framework (Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Mother Nature), it organises potential causes systematically before decision alternatives are generated. In extension it is used for diagnosing why a technology adoption programme underperformed, investigating causes of low crop yield, analysing reasons for poor attendance at training programmes, and improving the quality of service delivery.

4.5 Data-driven decision making (DDDM)
Data-driven decision making (DDDM) refers to basing decisions on the analysis of data rather than on intuition alone (Jones et al., 2017). In agricultural extension, DDDM enables evidence-based programme design, resource allocation and performance monitoring. The main data sources in agricultural extension are:

farm surveys and household data;
remote sensing and satellite imagery;
weather and climate data from meteorological agencies;
market price data and value chain analysis; and
extension programme monitoring and evaluation reports.

title: 5  Problem solving in agriculture and extension organisations
text:
5.1 What is a problem?
Problem solving is central to human activity in every field, but it takes on particular significance in agriculture and extension work, where poor decisions can affect livelihoods, food security and environmental sustainability. This chapter defines a problem, examines the problems extension workers face, sets out process frameworks for agricultural problem solving, and distinguishes problem solving from decision making.
Linhart (1976) defines a problem as an interactive relation between a subject and its surroundings, incorporating an inner conflict that is resolved by searching for transitions from an initial condition to a final, desired condition (the goal). A problem is therefore not merely a technical obstacle — it is a relational phenomenon arising in the gap between a person’s current capacity and the demands of their situation.
crumbs: 5  Problem solving in agriculture and extension organisations

title: 5  Problem solving in agriculture and extension organisations
text:
5.1.1 Three core properties of a problem
Linhart (1976) identifies three core properties of a problem:

Inner conflict as driver: the tension between current and desired states is not merely intellectual — it is motivational. In agricultural extension, unresolved problems such as crop losses or declining incomes are the motivational drivers for seeking new approaches.
Conflict creates activity: without the tension of an unsolved problem there is no impetus to act. The problem’s inner conflict is the engine of purposeful behaviour.
Transcending the given: the problem solver must exceed what is directly stated, searching beyond the current situation and the available information. This distinguishes genuine problem solving from routine task execution.



5.1.2 The problematic situation
Linhart (1976) defines the problematic situation as the totality of conditions that determine the formation and specific characteristics of a problem. These conditions may be static or dynamic, and their nature fundamentally shapes what kinds of solutions are possible (Table 5.1).



Table 5.1: Static and dynamic problematic situations










Aspect
Static problematic situation
Dynamic problematic situation




Definition

Nature

Unpredictable, open system


Example
Solving a mathematical puzzle
Managing a flood-affected paddy field


Strategy

Continuous adaptation; flexible, iterative strategies


Challenge
May not reflect real-world agricultural complexity
Requires ongoing monitoring; solutions may become obsolete












Key insight



In agriculture, most problems are dynamic rather than static. Rainfall, pest pressure, soil fertility, market prices and policy environments change simultaneously. Effective agricultural problem solving must be adaptive, iterative and grounded in ongoing observation.




5.1.3 Features of dynamic problem solving
The difficulties of acting in complex, changing situations have been widely documented (see Dörner, 1997). In agriculture, dynamic problem solving has the following features:

Change over time: problem conditions evolve continuously — a minor pest outbreak can escalate rapidly, and a drought can become a food security crisis within a season.
External influences: agricultural problems are shaped by natural forces, market dynamics, policy environments and technological change — none of which extension workers control.
Limited control: practitioners can often only respond to changes rather than prevent them, making adaptive capacity as important as pre-planned solutions.
Ongoing monitoring: continuous observation and adjustment are required; static plans rarely survive contact with actual conditions unchanged.
Positive potential: dynamic change occasionally reveals unexpected opportunities — late rains saving a wilting crop, or price spikes making a previously unviable crop profitable.

title: 5  Problem solving in agriculture and extension organisations
text:
5.2 Problem solving in extension organisations

5.2.1 The challenge for extension workers
Extension workers serve as the bridge between scientific knowledge systems and farming communities, operating simultaneously in institutional, social, technical and political domains (see Swanson & Rajalahti, 2010). As environments change rapidly — driven by technology, climate change, market liberalisation and shifting government priorities — the problems extension workers face become more complex and less predictable. At its core, a problem exists when an individual has a goal but lacks a clear method to achieve it (Newell & Simon, 1972). This distinguishes genuine problem solving from the routine application of learned procedures.


5.2.2 The five-step problem-solving process
A widely used sequential framework sets out five steps (Bormann & Bormann, 1988):

Define the problem clearly: describe the gap between the current and desired situation in specific, observable terms without implying solutions.
Formulate goals and criteria: establish what a good solution looks like before generating options. Criteria anchor the subsequent evaluation process.
Generate hypothetical solutions: produce multiple candidate solutions without premature evaluation. Quantity and variety at this stage improve the eventual quality of the choice.
Collect and analyse data: gather evidence that distinguishes between candidate solutions and confirms or disconfirms hypothesised causes.
Test solutions against criteria: evaluate each candidate, select the best fit, implement and monitor.



5.2.3 Problems of county extension agents: the West Virginia survey
A statewide survey of 48 extension agents across 38 counties of West Virginia in 1965 identified 126 problems (Table 5.2). The two most frequently cited — motivating leaders (18%) and motivating the public (16%) — are both people-problems requiring psychological and sociological insight, not technical knowledge alone.

5.2.4 The importance of problem definition
How a problem is framed determines what solutions appear possible. Albert Einstein is often quoted as observing that the formulation of a problem is more essential than its solution. Extension workers must therefore invest time in definition before rushing to solutions.






The power of reframing



Original framing: ‘How can we reach young homemakers?’ — this focuses on the extension worker’s logistics.
Reframed: ‘How can we free up time for young homemakers to attend meetings?’ — this reveals the real barrier: childcare.
Implication: providing childcare during meetings immediately becomes the solution.
Rule: frame problems in terms of controllable elements. ‘Not enough time’ is not actionable; task prioritisation and delegation are.




5.2.5 People-problems and the danger of mental set
Working with human attitudes and motivations is fundamentally different from diagnosing a crop disease. Extension workers need psychological and sociological concepts as analytical tools, not just agricultural expertise (Van den Ban & Hawkins, 1996).
Mental set — the tendency to apply familiar thinking patterns even when they no longer fit — is a major obstacle. Classic riddles illustrate this: ‘A farmer has 20 cows. All but 13 die. How many remain?’ (Answer: 13, not 7.) Extension workers must guard against applying solutions that worked in one context to structurally different problems. Strategies for overcoming mental set include:

Asking clarifying questions: ‘What exactly is the problem?’ ‘What are we assuming that we have not verified?’
Reasoning by analogy: how have other fields — health promotion, community organising — solved comparable problems of reaching disengaged populations?
Seeking diverse perspectives: people from different backgrounds hold different mental sets; cross-functional problem definition almost always reveals dimensions any one group would miss (Rogers, 2003).

section: 5.3 Problem solving: process and framework in agriculture
text:
5.3 Problem solving: process and framework in agriculture

5.3.1 A systems thinking approach
Agricultural problems are embedded in living systems characterised by complexity, variability and uncertainty. Effective agricultural problem solving must therefore be systematic while remaining flexible enough to accommodate inherent unpredictability. Systems thinking — understanding how components interact and how system-level properties emerge from these interactions — provides an essential conceptual foundation (Checkland, 1981). Its key principles are:

Feedback loops: actions generate consequences that loop back to influence future conditions. Excess fertiliser increases yield in the short term but degrades soil in the long term — a delayed negative feedback that a narrow analysis would miss.
Emergence: system-level problems (e.g., declining watershed health) emerge from many individual actions, none of which individually causes the outcome.
Delays: the consequences of agricultural decisions often appear long after the decision, making causal connections difficult to identify without systematic tracking.
Leverage points: some interventions produce disproportionately large improvements. Identifying high-leverage points is a core skill in agricultural problem solving (Senge, 1990).



5.3.2 The group problem-solving process
Many agricultural problems require collective, participatory solutions. The five-step group process adapts the general framework to the social dynamics of extension (Adams & Galanes, 2009), as shown in Table 5.3.

5. Implement and assess

section: 5.4 Problem solving and decision making: key differences
text:
5.4 Problem solving and decision making: key differences
Problem solving and decision making are related but distinct processes. Decision making is embedded within the larger process of problem solving — specifically during the ‘evaluate and choose’ stage. Problem solving asks ‘what is wrong and how can it be fixed?’; decision making asks ‘which of these available options should I choose?’ Decision making without prior problem solving risks selecting solutions to the wrong problem; problem solving without rigorous decision making risks an inability to commit to a course of action (see March, 1994). The differences are summarised in Table 5.5.



Table 5.5: Problem solving and decision making compared










Dimension
Problem solving
Decision making




Core question
What is wrong and why? How can the situation be improved?
Which available option best achieves the desired outcome?


Focus

Evaluating and selecting among defined alternatives


Scope
Broader — requires investigation and solution development
Narrower — assumes the problem is understood and options are known


Timing
Unfolds over extended periods as causes are investigated
Requires a focused, timely commitment to one course of action


Information
May require new data collection to understand the problem
Draws on existing information to compare alternatives


Outcome
Eliminates or reduces the root cause
Selects the best available option from those under consideration







5.4.1 Programmed and non-programmed decisions
Simon (1960) distinguishes two kinds of decisions:

Programmed decisions: routine, repetitive decisions for which standard procedures already exist — for example, an extension agent following an established pesticide application recommendation protocol.
Non-programmed decisions: novel, complex decisions requiring original analysis and judgement — for example, deciding how to respond to a newly emerged plant disease with no established recommendation.

Effective extension managers invest appropriate analytical effort and resist applying programmed responses to non-programmed situations — a temptation strengthened by the human preference for fast, intuitive judgement (Kahneman, 2011).

title: 6  Theories, models and techniques for problem solving
text:
6.1 Reflective thinking model
This chapter presents three classic models of problem solving — Dewey’s reflective thinking model, the Socratic model and Newell and Simon’s problem space model — followed by the main group techniques used in organisations (Six Thinking Hats and brainstorming) and creativity-based techniques, including lateral thinking and the management of cognitive biases.
Dewey (1933) defined reflective thinking as ‘active, persistent, and careful consideration of any belief or supposed form of knowledge in the light of the grounds that support it and the further conclusions to which it leads’. Reflection is not passive pondering but active inquiry: the thinker examines evidence for beliefs, considers alternative interpretations and follows reasoning to its conclusions. The cycle does not end with action — reflection on results feeds back into revised understanding (see also Schön, 1983).
crumbs: 6  Theories, models and techniques for problem solving

title: 6  Theories, models and techniques for problem solving
text:
6.1.1 Seven-step reflective thinking process

Define the problem: clearly identify what is problematic. The initial ‘felt difficulty’ must be precisely articulated before effective analysis can begin.
Analyse the problem: examine the available evidence. What is known? What is uncertain? What assumptions are being made?
Establish criteria: define what a satisfactory solution would look like before generating options.
Consider possible solutions: generate multiple candidates without premature evaluation. Intellectual openness at this stage is essential.
Decide on a solution: evaluate candidates against the established criteria and select the solution best supported by evidence and reasoning.
Implement the solution: execute the chosen course of action with awareness that implementation generates new information.
Follow up: monitor outcomes. Results feed back into a revised understanding of the problem.

title: 6  Theories, models and techniques for problem solving
section: 6.2 The Socratic model of problem solving
text:
6.2 The Socratic model of problem solving
Socrates employed questioning (elenchus) to expose contradictions in learners’ thoughts and guide them toward deeper understanding. Rather than lecturing, he asked apparently naive questions that forced his interlocutors to examine and revise beliefs they had held unquestioned. This approach — dialectical thinking — engages productively with contradictions to synthesise new understanding.

6.2.1 What Socratic questioning cultivates

Clarification: ‘What exactly do you mean?’ ‘Can you give an example?’
Probing assumptions: ‘What are you assuming?’ ‘Is this assumption always valid?’
Probing evidence: ‘What evidence supports this?’ ‘Are there alternative interpretations?’
Exploring implications: ‘If this is true, what follows?’ ‘What are the consequences?’



6.2.2 The three-stage dialectical mechanism

Identify contradictions: recognise where current assumptions clash with observed reality.
Explore tensions: understand why the contradictions exist — what different values or information sources underlie each position?
Synthesise: build a new, more comprehensive understanding that transcends the original contradiction.

title: 6  Theories, models and techniques for problem solving
section: 6.3 Newell and Simon’s problem space model
text:
6.3 Newell and Simon’s problem space model
Newell & Simon (1972) treat problem solving as a search process within a problem space — the complete set of possible states and transition pathways between the initial situation and the goal. The model laid the foundation for modern cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence. Its main concepts are illustrated in Table 6.1.



Table 6.1: Concepts of the problem space model with agricultural examples










Concept
Definition
Agricultural example

All combinations of variety, planting date, fertiliser rate and irrigation that could address a yield decline

The current, problematic situation

6.3.1 Key heuristic strategies

Means–end analysis: identify the largest gap between the current and goal state and select the operator most likely to reduce it; repeat until the goal is reached.
Hill climbing: always choose the operator that appears to move most directly toward the goal. This is efficient but prone to local optima.
Working backwards: begin from the goal state and reason backwards to identify the required prior steps.



6.3.2 Critiques

Well-structured bias: the model works best for problems with clearly defined states (puzzles, games) and is less effective for ill-structured problems, where goals and operators are ambiguous.
Neglect of emotion and culture: the model focuses purely on cognition; collective, culturally situated problem solving requires different frameworks.

6.4 Problem-solving techniques in organisations

6.4.1 Six Thinking Hats
De Bono’s (1985) Six Thinking Hats method addresses a fundamental limitation of conventional group discussion: people mix information, emotion, logic and creativity in ways that generate conflict rather than insight. The method separates different types of thinking in time — everyone thinks in the same direction simultaneously, but the direction changes as hats are ‘switched’. This parallel-thinking approach reduces defensiveness and generates richer analysis (Table 6.2).



Table 6.2: The Six Thinking Hats and their extension applications











Hat
Thinking mode
Focus
Extension application




White
Objective
Data and facts only — no interpretation or judgement
‘What data do we have on farmer adoption rates?’


Red
Emotional
Gut feelings and emotional responses without justification
‘My instinct says this intervention will face strong resistance.’


Black
Critical
Risks, weaknesses and reasons a proposal might fail
‘This requires farmers to invest before they see returns — cash flow is a barrier.’


Yellow
Optimistic
Benefits, advantages and best-case scenarios
‘If this works, it could reduce input costs by 40%.’


Green
Creative
New ideas, alternatives and lateral possibilities
‘What if we recruited the most sceptical farmer as co-designer?’


Blue
Process
Managing the thinking process itself; metacognition
Facilitator sets the agenda, sequences the hats and summarises












Recommended sequence for critical thinking




White Hat — establish the factual baseline;
Yellow Hat — identify genuine benefits;
Black Hat — identify genuine risks;
Green Hat — generate creative alternatives that capture the benefits while avoiding the risks;
Red Hat — capture gut reactions to the alternatives;
Blue Hat — summarise and plan the next steps.

Each round is time-limited to 2–5 minutes to maintain energy and focus.




6.4.2 Brainstorming
Osborn (1953) observed that conventional group meetings suppressed creativity because participants feared criticism and self-censored unconventional ideas. His solution was to separate idea generation from evaluation — suspending judgement to create psychological safety for unconventional thinking. Later research on group creativity has examined the conditions under which such groups actually outperform individuals (see Paulus & Nijstad, 2003). The use of brainstorming in decision making is discussed in Section 4.3.

Five core principles

Focus: maintain a clear focus on the specific problem. A brainstorm that drifts loses its generative power.
Suspended judgement: no criticism during generation — not even through body language. All ideas are recorded.
Personal safety: participants must be confident that expressing a ‘silly’ idea will not damage their standing.
Serial discussion: one person speaks at a time, which ensures that all ideas are heard and that quieter participants contribute.
Build on ideas: combine, modify and extend others’ contributions. The most valuable ideas in a brainstorm are often hybrids.



Three approaches to brainstorming

Visioning: imagine an ideal future unconstrained by current resources. Techniques include the Wish List, the Ideal Scenario and the Time Machine (‘It is 2040 and this problem has been brilliantly solved — what did we do?’).
Modifying: systematically examine current practices and ask how each element could be improved within real constraints. Customer utility maps identify pain points at each stage of the user experience.
Experimenting: combine existing elements in novel ways — ‘What if we combined SMS advisory with community listening groups?’ This is innovation through recombination rather than radical invention.

6.5 Creativity-based problem-solving techniques

6.5.1 Lateral thinking
Lateral thinking describes a deliberate approach to generating ideas by attacking problems from unexpected angles rather than following the conventional logic of ‘vertical thinking’ (de Bono, 1970). Vertical thinking deepens an existing line of reasoning; lateral thinking abandons it in search of a different starting point (Table 6.3).



Table 6.3: Vertical and lateral thinking compared










Dimension
Vertical thinking
Lateral thinking




Direction
Deepens and refines an existing approach
Generates alternative approaches and entry points


Judgement
Selective — accepts only what is logically valid
Generative — suspends judgement to explore unconventional possibilities


Best for
Optimising and refining known solutions
Generating novel solutions when known approaches have failed








6.5.2 Lateral thinking techniques

Random word: introduce an unrelated, randomly selected word and force connections to the problem. This short-circuits habitual thinking patterns.
Provocative operation (Po): make a deliberately outrageous statement — ‘Po: Farmers should pay for extension services with crops, not money.’ The provocation can lead to practical ideas such as value-sharing arrangements.
Reversal: reverse the problem. ‘How do we stop farmers from wanting to attend meetings?’ often reveals assumptions that are invisible in the original framing.
Challenge: systematically question every assumption in the current approach. Why does extension advice have to be delivered by trained agents? Why must training be in person?



6.5.3 Individual and group problem solving
The strengths and weaknesses of individual and group problem solving are compared in Table 6.4 (compare Table 3.1 for decision making).



Table 6.4: Individual and group problem solving compared










Factor
Individual problem solving
Group problem solving




Strengths
Speed; freedom from social pressure; depth of focused thinking; avoids groupthink
Diverse knowledge; division of labour; mutual error-correction; greater implementation buy-in


Weaknesses
Limited knowledge base; cognitive blind spots; no correction mechanism
Social pressure toward conformity; dominance by high-status members; coordination costs


Best for
Well-defined technical problems within an individual’s expertise
Complex, multi-dimensional problems requiring diverse knowledge; community-accepted solutions








6.5.4 Cognitive biases in problem solving
Judgement under uncertainty is shaped by systematic biases (Kahneman, 2011; Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). Four are especially relevant to agricultural problem solving:

Gambler’s fallacy: the mistaken belief that past random events influence future random events — for example, believing that a drought is ‘due’ because it has not rained for weeks. Agricultural risk management requires an understanding of statistical independence.
Winner’s curse: the tendency to over-invest in a solution because competitive dynamics create pressure, regardless of whether it is appropriate for local conditions.
Confirmation bias: attending to evidence that confirms pre-existing beliefs while discounting contrary evidence. An agent convinced that a particular variety is superior will unconsciously filter new information accordingly.
Availability heuristic: judging the probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind. A dramatic crop failure will seem more likely to recur than the statistics justify.



6.5.5 Heuristics as problem-solving strategies
Heuristics and related strategies, together with their limitations, are summarised in Table 6.5.



Table 6.5: Heuristics as problem-solving strategies











Heuristic
Description
Agricultural application
Potential limitation




Trial and error
Systematically try solutions until one works
Testing pest control methods sequentially
Time-consuming; may cause harm during trials


Algorithm
Precise, step-by-step procedure producing the correct result
Soil testing and fertiliser recommendation protocol
Works only for well-defined problems


Working backwards
Start from the desired outcome and identify prior steps
‘To achieve food security by March, what must be planted by October?’
Requires a clear goal specification


Satisficing
Choose the first option meeting minimum acceptable criteria
Recommend the first feasible practice that yields adequate improvement
May miss significantly better solutions

7.1 Why these tools are introduced here
This chapter introduces the data-based tools used to define, measure and diagnose problems — Voice of the Customer, Critical to Quality measures, line graphs, control charts, Pareto charts, the fishbone diagram and the 5 Whys — together with the development of countermeasures, the Balanced Scorecard, personality-based problem-solving preferences and the E5 framework for organisational problem solving.
The statistical and graphical tools in this chapter — control charts, Pareto charts and fishbone diagrams — originate from quality improvement traditions, particularly Total Quality Management (TQM) and Six Sigma (Deming, 1986; Juran, 1951). They are included here not to import Six Sigma as a separate subject, but because these tools are the most widely validated methods for the measurement and root-cause-analysis phases of problem solving — essential disciplines for any organisation, including agricultural extension. The Six Sigma DMAIC cycle (Define → Measure → Analyse → Improve → Control) provides a logical organising framework showing which tool belongs to which phase of problem diagnosis (Table 7.1, Figure 7.1).

7.2 Voice of the Customer (VOC)
The Voice of the Customer (VOC) is a structured process of capturing the expressed and latent needs, expectations and complaints of those served. In agricultural extension, the direct customers are the farmers who receive advisory services; indirect customers include government departments, funders and communities. VOC data are gathered through interviews, focus groups, surveys, direct observation and complaint analysis. Raw data are processed to extract specific customer requirements — statements of what is needed, free of solution language — which are then translated into measurable specifications through CTQ analysis.

7.3 Critical to Quality (CTQ) measures
CTQ measures translate qualitative customer language — ‘I want faster advice’ — into quantitative operational targets — ‘Response within 48 hours in 95% of cases.’ There are three levels:

Customer requirement — what the farmer expresses;
Drivers — the key dimensions that underlie the requirement; and
CTQ measure — a specific, measurable standard for each driver.

Without CTQ measures, quality improvement efforts lack direction and measurable targets.

7.4 Line graphs
A line graph plots data points collected at regular intervals and connects them sequentially, making trends, patterns and turning points immediately visible. In problem analysis, line graphs display baseline performance, monitor the trajectory of a problem and visualise the effect of an intervention. Upward or downward trends, flat lines, sudden spikes and cyclical patterns each carry a distinct diagnostic meaning. In agricultural extension, many problems have seasonal signatures that a line graph immediately reveals.

title: 7  Statistical and graphical methods and the E5 framework for problem solving
text:
7.5 Control charts (statistical process control)
Invented by Walter A. Shewhart at Bell Laboratories in the 1920s (Shewhart, 1931), the control chart is the most analytically powerful graphical tool in this chapter. Its value lies in distinguishing two fundamentally different types of variation:

Common cause variation: predictable, inherent variation that is always present in any process — the normal output of the existing system. It does not require corrective action; it requires system-level redesign if it is deemed unsatisfactory. Treating common cause variation as special cause variation creates instability and wastes effort (Deming, 1986).
Special cause variation: unusual, sporadic variation triggered by a specific, identifiable external factor, which appears as data points outside the control limits. It demands investigation and correction.







Control limit calculation



\[
\text{CL} = \bar{x}, \qquad \text{UCL} = \bar{x} + 3s, \qquad \text{LCL} = \bar{x} - 3s
\]
where \(\bar{x}\) is the mean of all data points (the Centre Line) and \(s\) is the standard deviation.
Worked example: average agent visit time = 24.9 min; standard deviation = 6.9 min.

UCL = 24.9 + (3 × 6.9) = 24.9 + 20.7 = 45.6 min
LCL = 24.9 − (3 × 6.9) = 24.9 − 20.7 = 4.2 min

Any day outside these limits is a special cause requiring investigation.

text:
7.6 Pareto charts
The Pareto principle — that approximately 80% of effects arise from 20% of causes — guides practitioners to focus limited resources on the ‘vital few’ causes rather than dispersing effort across all possible causes (Juran, 1951). A Pareto chart displays categories of causes in descending order of frequency (bars on the left Y-axis) with a cumulative percentage line (right Y-axis) that rises from left to right. Categories to the left of the 80% threshold on the cumulative line are the vital few — the highest-leverage improvement targets. Stratification using a second Pareto chart then breaks the biggest category into sub-causes, connecting directly to the fishbone diagram.

7.8 The 5 Whys technique
Developed by Sakichi Toyoda and central to the Toyota Production System (Ohno, 1988), the 5 Whys technique peels back layers of causation by asking ‘Why?’ repeatedly until an actionable root cause — not merely a symptom — is reached.






5 Whys example



Problem: ran through a red light.

Why? → Late for work.
Why? → Woke up late.
Why? → The alarm did not work.
Why? → The battery was exhausted.
Why? → Forgot to check it.

Root cause: no routine for maintaining personal equipment. Countermeasure: a monthly calendar reminder to check the alarm battery.
Lesson: what appeared to be a traffic violation was a failure of a personal maintenance habit. Issues that seem technical frequently turn out to be human and process problems.


Unvalidated root causes lead teams to pursue worthless countermeasures, wasting time and resources. Root causes identified through diagramming and questioning must therefore be verified with actual data (correlation analysis, designed experiments or stratified data analysis) before countermeasures are developed.

title: 7  Statistical and graphical methods and the E5 framework for problem solving
text:
7.9 Developing and evaluating countermeasures
A countermeasure is a targeted action designed to eliminate a confirmed root cause. Each candidate countermeasure is evaluated against two criteria:

Effectiveness — how completely and permanently does it prevent the root cause from recurring?
Feasibility — how practical is it given the available resources, time and capacity?

Countermeasures are plotted on a two-axis prioritisation matrix; those scoring high on both axes are immediate priorities. After implementation, control charts and line graphs confirm whether improvement has occurred. If it has, the new process is standardised — documented, trained and embedded in operating procedures to prevent regression.

text:
7.10 The Balanced Scorecard (BSC)
Developed by Kaplan & Norton (1992), the Balanced Scorecard translates organisational vision and strategy into performance measures across four perspectives:

Financial: how do we appear to funders?
Customer/farmer: how do we appear to those we serve?
Internal process: what processes must we excel at?
Learning and growth: how will we sustain our capacity?

The BSC ensures that operational improvements from TQM tools are aligned with strategic intent — diagnosing what is broken and fixing it in a way that advances organisational goals.

text:
7.11 Personality types and problem-solving preferences
Research using the Myers–Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) demonstrates that different personality dimensions align with distinct problem-solving strategies (Huitt, 1992). Extroverts prefer brainstorming and thinking aloud; introverts prefer private reflection and incubation. Sensing types favour inductive reasoning from facts; intuitive types prefer deductive reasoning and visualisation. Thinking types gravitate toward analysis and task breakdown; feeling types toward values clarification. Judging types prefer evaluation and backward planning; perceiving types prefer brainstorming and taking another’s perspective. For extension facilitators, this means structuring groups for cognitive diversity, allowing individual idea generation before group discussion, and recognising that different phases of problem solving benefit from different personality orientations.

text:
7.12 The E5 framework: a comprehensive organisational problem-solving model
The E5 framework provides a structured, five-phase approach to solving complex organisational problems. It is distinguished by its emphasis on deep problem understanding before solution development — the most common failure point in organisational problem solving (Table 7.2).



Table 7.2: Phases of the E5 framework











Phase
Name
Core activity
Key tools




1
Expand
Framestorming — explore the problem from every angle before committing to any definition; diverse team; ‘What if…?’ and ‘How might we…?’ questions
Six Thinking Hats; brainstorming; VOC


2
Examine
Identify root causes via the Iceberg Model: surface events → patterns → systemic structures → mental models
Fishbone diagram; 5 Whys; Pareto charts


3
Empathize
Map all stakeholders; create empathy maps (Say/Think/Feel/Do); conduct interviews to gather real perspectives
Empathy mapping; stakeholder analysis


4
Elevate
Apply the Four-Frame Model (structural, human resources, political, symbolic) to connect the problem to organisational dynamics
Bolman and Deal’s Four-Frame Model


5
Envision
Design the future through backcasting: ideal future state → required milestones → prioritised action plan
Backcasting; Balanced Scorecard






The Iceberg Model used in the Examine phase draws on systems thinking (Section 5.3.1), in which visible events are traced to underlying patterns, structures and mental models (Senge, 1990).

7.12.1 The Four-Frame Model in the Elevate phase
The Four-Frame Model (Bolman & Deal, 2017) diagnoses organisational problems from four complementary perspectives:

Structural: systems, roles, hierarchies and coordination mechanisms. Problems are diagnosed as misaligned structures or unclear roles.
Human resources: people’s needs, motivations and relationships. Problems are diagnosed as unmet needs, skill gaps or leadership failures.
Political: power, interests, coalitions and competition for resources. Problems are diagnosed as conflicts of interest or power imbalances.
Symbolic: culture, values, rituals and shared meanings. Problems are diagnosed as cultural misalignment or erosion of trust.



7.12.2 Case study: Omega Soundscapes






Case study: Omega Soundscapes



Omega Soundscapes, a premium headphone manufacturer, experienced a significant decline in sales. Leadership assumed that a recent price increase was the cause. Applying the E5 framework revealed the following:

Expand: framestorming generated alternative explanations, including quality decline, competition and brand perception.
Examine: the Iceberg Model uncovered that a cost-cutting decision had substituted cheaper components and that brand overconfidence had reduced quality monitoring.
Empathize: empathy maps showed customers, distributors and investors all experiencing different manifestations of declining perceived value.
Elevate: the Four-Frame analysis revealed structural coordination failures between R&D and marketing, declining sales-team morale, rigid financial policies overriding quality concerns, and a gap between the brand’s self-image and customer experience.
Envision: the team set a goal of 10% sales recovery within 12 months and backcasted a phased plan — quality audits and restoration (months 1–3), brand campaigns and R&D–marketing integration (months 4–8), and new product launches and distributor rebuilding (months 9–12).









Key reminder



Problem solving is not a straight line. New information at any phase may require returning to an earlier phase. The value of the E5 framework lies not in rigid sequence compliance but in the discipline of comprehensive problem understanding before commitment to a solution.
